blocks.text: “I declare,” he says. “I seriously declare that, until this crime is uncovered and punished by the law, I almost feel as if there were a stain on my name. Here is a gentleman who gave a large part of his life to me. He is a gentleman who gave the last day of his life to me, and a gentleman who sat at my table and slept under my roof again and again. He goes from my house to his own, and within an hour of leaving my house he is struck down. I cannot deny that he may have been followed from my house and watched at my house. He may even have been chosen as a target first because of his connection with my house. That connection may have made him seem to have greater wealth, and to be altogether more important, than his own quiet, modest manner would have shown. If I cannot use my wealth, my influence, and my position to bring everyone who committed such a crime out into the light, then I fail. I fail to show firmly my respect for that gentleman's memory, and I fail in my loyalty towards someone who was always loyal to me.”

He makes this firm declaration with great emotion and seriousness. As he speaks, he looks around the room as if he were speaking to a large meeting. At the same time, Mr. Bucket gives him a quick look that is watchful and serious. There might be a touch of pity in that look, if thinking such a thing were not far too bold.

“Today's ceremony,” Sir Leicester continues, “showed in a remarkable way how much the finest people in the country respected my dead friend.” He stresses that last word, because death removes all differences and puts everyone on the same level. “That ceremony, I say, has made the shock I have suffered from this most horrible and extremely bold crime even worse. If my own brother had committed it, I would not spare him.”
Mr. Bucket looks very serious. Volumnia says that the dead man was the most trustworthy and dearest person!
“You must feel it as a great loss to you, miss, no doubt,” Mr. Bucket replies in a gentle, comforting voice. “He was just the sort of man to be a great loss, I'm sure he was.”

In reply, Volumnia lets Mr. Bucket know that her sensitive mind is completely made up never to get over it as long as she lives. She also lets him know that her nerves are badly shaken forever, and that she does not expect at all to smile again. Meanwhile, she folds up a note into the three-cornered shape called a cocked hat. It is for that impressive old general at Bath whom people both respect and fear. The note describes her sad and gloomy condition.
“It gives a sudden shock to a delicate woman,” says Mr. Bucket with sympathy, “but it'll slowly pass.”

More than anything else, Volumnia wants to know what is being done. She wants to know whether they are going to find that terrible soldier guilty in court—convict him, or whatever it is. She also wants to know whether he had any helpers in the crime—accomplices, or whatever the thing is called in the law. And she asks a great deal more of the same simple, innocent kind.

“Why, you see, miss,” Mr. Bucket replies, using his finger in a convincing way. He is naturally so warm and attentive toward women that he had almost called her “my dear.” He goes on, “It isn't easy to answer those questions at this moment. Not at this moment. I've stayed on this case morning, noon, and night, Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet.” Here Mr. Bucket brings Sir Leicester into the conversation, because his importance gives him that right. “Without a glass or two of sherry, I don't think I could have kept my mind stretched and working as hard as it has been. I could answer your questions, miss, but my duty does not allow it. Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, will very soon be told everything that has been followed and found out. And I hope that he may find it—” Mr. Bucket looks serious again, “—to his satisfaction.”

The weak, worn-out cousin only hopes that some fellow will be put to death as an example. He compares getting a man hanged these days with getting a man a position paying ten thousand a year. He thinks that getting a man hanged needs more influence with powerful people. He has no doubt that, as an example, it is far better to hang the wrong fellow than no fellow.
